title: Generics & launch 8: Artworks
disclaimer: An educational course for project management of generic launches. It is not regulatory, legal or quality advice: EU rules are the anchor, and national and company practice vary.

blocks.markdown:
## Text first, artwork second

Everything printed on a pack or a leaflet starts as approved text: the SmPC, the labelling text and the PIL. These follow the **QRD template** (*modèle QRD*), the EMA's standard headings and wording. The template is used in centralised procedures and, with national notes, in MRP and DCP. **Artwork** (*maquette, artwork*) is how that approved text appears on the physical pack.

blocks.alt: Flow from QRD template to approved English texts, national translations, artwork per country, and printed carton, leaflet and blister foil
blocks.caption: From SmPC text to printed pack

blocks.alt: A page of the EMA QRD product-information template: SmPC section headings 1 to 4.2, with standard statements in angle brackets, placeholders in curly brackets and guidance notes in green
blocks.caption: The QRD template: fixed headings and standard wording (SmPC, version 10.4)

blocks.markdown:
## Why the distinction matters

Text is regulatory: it's approved during the procedure, and changes need a variation or a notification. Artwork is the design: layout, fonts and colours, with the text placed exactly. If the artwork shows a word that differs from the approved text, that's a compliance problem, not a design detail.

## When texts become final

In a DCP, the English texts are agreed by day 210 (Module 2). The translations follow in the national phase, and only after that can country artworks be finalised. Many teams prepare artwork drafts during the clock-stops, so they're ready when the texts are final.

**What this means for the launch timeline:** artwork can only be finalised once the translated texts are approved, and printing comes after that. Prepare drafts early to keep the launch from waiting on the printer.

The graphic design of the pack and leaflet showing the approved texts exactly. FR: maquette (artwork).

## Showing the agency what the pack will look like

EU law requires the application to include **mock-ups** (*maquettes*): flat, full-colour layouts of the outer and immediate packaging. Some agencies also ask for **specimens** (*spécimens*), meaning actual printed samples, later on.

blocks.alt: Schematic flat carton mock-up showing front panel, side with 2D code area, back panel with Blue Box position, and the die-line around it
blocks.caption: Anatomy of a mock-up

blocks.markdown:
## What a mock-up shows

A mock-up shows the real layout:

- front, sides and back
- fonts and colours
- where the Blue Box, the Braille and the 2D code go

The flat carton is drawn inside its **die-line** (*plan de découpe*), the technical drawing of cut and fold lines from the packaging site.

## Changes after approval

If a label or leaflet change isn't linked to the SmPC, for example a layout change, it can go through an **Art. 61(3) notification** (*notification article 61(3)*). The change can be made if the agency doesn't object within 90 days. Changes to the SmPC itself need a variation.
**What this means for the launch timeline:** mock-ups are needed during or right after the procedure, depending on the country. Plan them alongside the translations, not after the licence.

## Two features of every EU carton

Each country can require extra information on the pack, printed in a framed area called the **Blue Box** (*encadré bleu*). EU law also requires the product name in **Braille** (*braille*) on the carton.

blocks.alt: Schematic carton with a framed Blue Box area for national particulars, and a panel of embossed Braille dots for the product name
blocks.caption: Blue Box and Braille

blocks.markdown:
## The Blue Box

The Blue Box contains national particulars, for example the legal status, local product codes or reimbursement information. The CMDh publishes each country's requirements. Because the Blue Box differs by country, it's one of the main reasons each country needs its own pack (Lesson 6).

## Braille

The product name must appear in Braille on the outer packaging. Guidance recommends adding the strength where several strengths exist. The MAH must also make the leaflet available in formats suitable for blind and partially sighted people on request from patient organisations. Braille is embossed during carton printing, so it must be in the artwork and checked at proof stage.
**What this means for the launch timeline:** collect the Blue Box requirements for every target country before artwork starts. A missed national particular means a reprint.

cards.back: A framed area on the carton for country-specific particulars (CMDh list per country). FR: encadré bleu.
The product name must appear in Braille on the carton (Art. 56a); strength recommended where several exist.

questions.stem: Why does the Blue Box make multi-country packs harder?
options: Each country can require different particulars in it
questions.explanation: National particulars differ, so one shared carton must fit every country's Blue Box.

## Can patients actually use the leaflet?

The patient leaflet must reflect consultations with target patient groups. In practice, that means **readability testing** (*test de lisibilité*), also called user testing: real people try to find and understand key information in the draft leaflet.

blocks.alt: Loop from a draft leaflet to a test round, revision and re-test until the criteria are met, then a report for the dossier
blocks.caption: Readability (user) testing of the leaflet

blocks.markdown:
## How it typically works

Participants answer questions using the leaflet. A common success standard is that 90% of participants find each key piece of information, and 90% of those understand it. Failed items are rewritten and tested again.

## For generics: bridging

A generic's leaflet is usually very close to the reference product's. Often the applicant can **bridge** (*bridging*) to the reference product's tested leaflet, or to another already-tested leaflet, with a justification. That avoids a full new test.
**What this means for the launch timeline:** a full user test takes weeks. Check early whether a bridging justification is acceptable for your product.

cards.back: Testing the leaflet with real users to confirm they can find and understand key information (Art. 59(3)). FR: test de lisibilité.
Justifying that a leaflet is close enough to an already-tested one, instead of running a new test.

questions.stem: What does a common readability success standard require?
options: 90% find each key point, and 90% of those understand it
questions.explanation: The test measures whether information can be found and understood, not taste.

## A passport for every pack

To stop falsified medicines reaching patients, EU prescription medicines carry two **safety features** (*dispositifs de sécurité*): a **unique identifier** in a 2D DataMatrix code, and an **anti-tampering device** (*dispositif antieffraction*) that shows whether the pack has been opened. These have applied since 9 February 2019.

blocks.alt: Illustrative 2D code with its data (product code, serial number, batch, expiry, national number), the anti-tampering seal, and the flow from MAH upload to national system to pharmacy check
blocks.caption: Serialisation under the Falsified Medicines Directive

blocks.markdown:
## How the system works

1. The MAH, through the packager, prints a unique code on each pack.
2. It uploads the codes to the EU hub, which passes them to the national verification systems.
3. At dispensing, the pharmacy scans the pack. The system confirms it's genuine and marks it as dispensed (decommissioned).

A code that doesn't match triggers an alert.

## What a PM must arrange

Before the first pack ships, the following must be in place:

- the MAH's onboarding with the European hub organisation
- product master data uploaded for each country
- packaging lines able to print and verify codes
- carton space reserved for the code

Missing onboarding means packs can't be dispensed, even if they're perfectly made.
**What this means for the launch timeline:** onboarding with the European hub and uploading product data take weeks. Start them well before launch, and confirm the data reaches each national system.

cards.back: The 2D DataMatrix code on each pack: product code, serial number, batch, expiry and, where required, a national number.
A seal showing whether the pack has been opened. FR: dispositif antieffraction.
Marking a pack as dispensed in the national system when the pharmacy scans it.

questions.stem: Packs are made and released, but the MAH's product data was never uploaded. What happens at the pharmacy?
options: Scanning fails or raises an alert, so the pack can't be properly dispensed
questions.explanation: Verification needs the codes in the system. Without upload, the pack fails at the pharmacy.

## One pack for several countries

The particulars must be in the official language of each country where the pack is sold. A pack can carry several languages, as long as every language gives the same particulars. That's a **multilingual pack** (*conditionnement multilingue*).

blocks.alt: Pros and cons of multilingual packs: fewer pack versions and simpler runs versus limited carton space, national Blue Box and codes per country, and agreed wording
blocks.caption: One pack, several countries: multilingual packs

blocks.markdown:
## The trade-off

**Pros:** fewer pack versions (SKUs), bigger packaging runs, and stock that can move between countries.

**Cons:** limited carton space, a different Blue Box and different codes per country, and the need for every country's wording to fit. Multilingual packs are common for groups of smaller markets.

## Practical checks

Before choosing a multilingual pack, check:

- that the carton is big enough
- that every country accepts it
- that the Blue Box items can coexist
- that the serialisation data reaches every relevant national system

These checks are practice; national rules decide.

**What this means for the launch timeline:** deciding single-country or multilingual packs early changes the artwork count, the packaging runs and the stock planning. Make it a decision on the plan, not an afterthought.

cards.back: One pack carrying the same particulars in several languages, for several countries (Art. 63(1)). FR: conditionnement multilingue.
Stock-keeping unit: one distinct pack version. Multilingual packs reduce their number.

questions.stem: What's the main constraint on multilingual packs?
options: Carton space for all languages, plus each country's Blue Box and codes
questions.explanation: The carton has a fixed size, and every country's particulars must fit legibly.

## From approved text to first printed pack

Each country's artwork goes through the same loop. Most artwork delays come from late text approvals and rounds of corrections, not from design.

blocks.alt: Six steps: brief with texts and die-line; design; proofreading against approved text incl. Braille and codes; RA, QA and marketing approval; printer proof and print run; first-print inspection
blocks.caption: The artwork workflow

blocks.markdown:
### Process card: Country artwork

- What it is: creating and approving the printed packaging (carton, leaflet, blister foil) for one country
- Who owns it: the artwork or packaging coordinator; RA approves the texts, QA approves for GMP, and marketing approves the design
- Inputs: approved translated texts, the die-line from the packaging site, Blue Box requirements, the serialisation area, Braille
- Output: approved artwork, printer proofs, printed materials delivered to the packaging site
- Typical duration: weeks per country, longer with many correction rounds
- What makes it slip: late text approval, wrong die-line, proofreading errors found late, printer capacity
- PM watch-points: start drafts in the clock-stops, use one approved text source, and track every country's artwork as a separate line on the plan

## Proofreading is a GMP control

**Proofreading** (*relecture*) compares the artwork word by word with the approved text, and checks the Braille, the codes and the colours. Printing errors on packaging can lead to recalls, which is why it's controlled under GMP.
**What this means for the launch timeline:** artwork is often on the critical path in the last months before launch. Track text approval, proof rounds and printer slots for every country.

cards.back: A word-by-word check of the artwork against the approved text, plus Braille, codes and colours. A GMP control. FR: relecture.
The technical drawing of the carton's cut and fold lines, from the packaging site. FR: plan de découpe.

## Artwork follows the licence

Every time the approved texts change, through a variation or an Art. 61(3) notification, the artwork changes too. Each country's pack then has a new artwork version, and a date by which it must be in use.

blocks.alt: Timeline of artwork versions v1 at launch, v2 after a safety variation and v3 for a new pack size, with an implementation deadline question about old stock
blocks.caption: Artwork versions follow the licence

blocks.markdown:
## What to track per country

- **Approved text version:** which approval it comes from.
- **Artwork version:** linked to that text version.
- **Implementation deadline:** the date from which new packs must carry the new texts. Safety-related changes are usually implemented faster.
- **Old stock:** whether packs with old texts may still be released, until when, and under which conditions.

These implementation rules vary by country and by type of change.

## Why it matters at launch

A variation approved just before launch can make freshly printed cartons obsolete. Before printing, check whether any text change is pending in any country.
**What this means for the launch timeline:** ask RA before every print order: is any text change pending? Printing just before a text change wastes material, and can delay launch.

cards.back: Linking each artwork version to an approved text version, with implementation dates and old-stock rules per country.
The date from which packs must carry the updated approved texts. Usually shorter for safety changes.

questions.stem: A safety variation is approved two weeks before launch. What should the PM check first?
options: Whether the printed packaging still matches the approved texts, and the implementation deadline
questions.explanation: Printed materials may already be outdated. The implementation rules decide whether they can still be used.
